title: Tenali and the Mirror

full_text:
As King Krishnadevaraya approached his fiftieth year, he noticed silver strands appearing in his hair and subtle lines around his eyes. A melancholy gloom settled over the Emperor. He refused to look into mirrors, banished all grey-haired servants from his presence, and spent thousands of gold coins on charlatans who promised alchemical elixirs of perpetual youth.

The court ministers worried as state matters were neglected while the King bathed in herbal oils and brooded over his reflection.

Tenali Raman resolved to heal the King’s soul.
Tenali commissioned a master glassmaker to craft an extraordinary bronze hand mirror. The glass was polished with exceptional clarity, but around its ornate silver frame, Tenali had four miniature scenes carved in relief:
At the bottom: A young sprout breaking through the soil;
On the right: A blooming lotus in full summer glory;
At the top: A golden banyan tree laden with sweet fruit sheltering travelers;
On the left: A peaceful river flowing gracefully into the eternal ocean.

Tenali brought the mirror to the King's bedchamber:
'Maharaj, I have brought the Mirror of True Age, which reveals the eternal truth of royalty.'

The King hesitated, then looked into the glass.
He saw his silvering hair, his seasoned brow, and the lines of fifty years of leadership.
He frowned: 'Tenali, this mirror shows my aging face; why dost thou call it miraculous?'

Tenali knelt and pointed gently to the carved frame:
'Maharaj, look at the four seasons carved around your reflection:
When a man is twenty, he is like the green sprout—full of raw energy, but easily swayed by winds.
When he is thirty, he is the blooming lotus—dazzling, but preoccupied with his own splendor.
When he reaches fifty, Maharaj, he becomes the Golden Banyan Tree!
His silver hairs are the deep roots of experience; his lines are the branches of wisdom that shelter thousands of subjects from storms!
And in his twilight, he is the calm river that enriches the entire earth before merging with eternity.

Would Your Majesty trade the majesty of a sheltering banyan tree for the weak sprout of a youth who has never fought a battle or governed an empire?
Grey hair on a wise king is not a blemish; it is the silver crown of wisdom placed upon his head by heaven itself!'

Tears filled King Krishnadevaraya’s eyes as Tenali’s profound philosophical words touched his heart.
The heavy cloud of vanity and fear lifted from the Emperor's spirit.
He smiled, embracing Tenali with deep gratitude:
'Tenali, thou hast restored my dignity as a man and my purpose as a king!'

The King threw away the fraudulent youth potions, returned to the diwan with renewed energy, and governed his people with the ripe, loving wisdom of the Golden Banyan Tree.
moral: Accepting the natural passage of time with grace and wisdom brings true dignity that false youth cannot buy.
